page.mentor_intro: High-altitude pulmonary edema is the deadliest of the acute altitude illnesses and the one most often missed early, because its first symptoms — exertional dyspnoea, cough, reduced exercise tolerance — look like simple fatigue at altitude. It is a non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema driven by hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, arriving one to five days after ascent, and it is preventable with graded ascent and treatable with descent and oxygen. Every physician advising travellers, trekkers, or workers deploying to altitude should know its time course, its susceptibility patterns, and the absolute priority of not waiting for it to 'settle'.

teaching_points.claim: Three forms of acute altitude illness — acute mountain sickness, high-altitude cerebral oedema and high-altitude pulmonary oedema — can each arise 1–5 days after ascent to altitudes of 2500 m or higher.
HAPE is a non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema resulting from excessive hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, rather than left-heart failure.

The prevalence of acute altitude illness varies with acclimatisation status, rate of ascent and individual susceptibility; chronic mountain sickness affects permanent high-altitude resident populations.
Clinical frameworks exist for counselling and evaluating patients before travel to altitude and for the prevention and treatment of the main forms of acute altitude illness.

uncertainties: Pharmacological prophylaxis choices (nifedipine, PDE5 inhibitors, acetazolamide) for HAPE-susceptible individuals are not fully standardised.
The relative roles of descent, portable hyperbaric chambers and in-situ oxygen in moderate HAPE are guided mainly by observational experience.
mcq_angles: Time window (1–5 days) and altitude threshold (≥2500 m) for acute altitude illness.
Pathophysiology: hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction producing non-cardiogenic oedema.
Distinguishing HAPE from cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and pneumonia at altitude.
Prevention strategies: graded ascent, acclimatisation days, avoiding rapid gain in sleeping altitude.
case_hooks: A trekker develops exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough on day 2 at 4200 m and wants to push on to the summit; decide the management and the rule for continued ascent.
A patient with a previous episode of HAPE asks whether they can join a high-altitude expedition and what prophylaxis is appropriate.
page.gaps: Drug dosing (nifedipine, acetazolamide, tadalafil), Lake Louise diagnostic criteria detail, and disposition thresholds are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against the Wilderness Medical Society guideline before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Choosing between high-flow nasal oxygen, CPAP and bilevel NIV in acute hypoxaemic failure is now one of the most consequential triage decisions in the ICU, because the wrong choice does not merely fail — it delays intubation past the point where it helps. The first official clinical practice guideline on non-invasive respiratory support has been published specifically because modality selection was so variable. Knowing what each device does physiologically, when each is indicated, and how to recognise failure early is core competency for any physician managing acute respiratory failure.

teaching_points.claim: Non-invasive respiratory support strategies — HFNC, NIV and CPAP — may prevent intubation and improve outcomes in acute hypoxaemic and hypercapnic respiratory failure, but uncertainty about optimal patient and modality selection led to the first official clinical practice guideline.

High-flow nasal therapy provides low-level positive airway pressure, anatomical dead-space washout, good tolerance, and can be used during breaks from CPAP or BiPAP; CPAP and BiPAP deliver distinct physiological effects and require interface- and settings-specific expertise.

Extubation failure — reintubation within 2–7 days of planned extubation — is associated with prolonged ventilation, increased ventilator-associated pneumonia, longer ICU and hospital stays, and increased mortality.
High-quality evidence guiding HFNC discontinuation is lacking; weaning of flow, FiO2, or both is largely left to clinician discretion, and failure to de-escalate has measurable consequences.

uncertainties: Which hypoxaemic patients benefit from NIV versus HFNC first-line, and how to identify those in whom NIV merely delays intubation, remain contested.
Optimal HFNC weaning and liberation protocols (what to reduce first, how fast) are not evidence-defined.
mcq_angles: Physiological comparison: HFNC (dead-space washout, low PEEP) versus CPAP/BiPAP.
Post-extubation failure definition (reintubation within 2–7 days) and its consequences.
Guideline-based modality selection for hypoxaemic versus hypercapnic failure.
Recognising NIRS failure and indications to escalate to intubation.
case_hooks: A patient with severe hypoxaemic pneumonia is started on HFNC; outline what you monitor to decide whether intubation is needed, and when NIV would have been the wrong choice.
A COPD patient is extubated after an exacerbation; choose and justify the post-extubation respiratory support and the criteria for reintubation.
page.gaps: Specific intubation-trigger scores (ROX index, HACOR), interface selection detail and ventilator settings tables are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against the full ATS/ERS/JRS guideline before approval.

page.mentor_intro: High-flow nasal cannula oxygen has moved from novelty to first-line therapy in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure within a decade, because it does several things simple oxygen cannot: it washes out anatomical dead space, generates a small positive-pressure effect, delivers a constant FiO2, and is comfortable enough that patients actually keep it on. The European Respiratory Society guideline formalises where the evidence supports it, the Cochrane review and meta-analysis quantify the benefit versus conventional oxygen, and understanding the device physiology is what lets you use it intelligently rather than reflexively.

teaching_points.claim: The ERS clinical practice guideline provides GRADE-based recommendations for HFNC alongside other non-invasive forms of respiratory support in adults with acute respiratory failure.

HFNC uses an air/oxygen blender, active humidifier and heated single tube to deliver flows up to 60 L/min, with physiological advantages including reduced anatomical dead space, a PEEP effect, constant FiO2 and good humidification.
A Cochrane systematic review evaluates HFNC versus standard oxygen therapy or non-invasive ventilation for adults with, or at risk of, acute respiratory failure in the ICU.
Meta-analysis of randomised trials compares HFNC with conventional oxygen therapy specifically in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, pooling safety and efficacy outcomes.

uncertainties: The evidence base for HFNC in hypercapnic respiratory failure is separate and less mature than for hypoxaemic failure.
Optimal flow and FiO2 titration, and objective thresholds for escalation, are not standardised across studies.
mcq_angles: HFNC components and physiological effects (dead-space washout, PEEP, constant FiO2, humidification).

page.mentor_intro: A hip fracture is never just an orthopaedic problem — it is a whole-patient event that lands on an older adult with multiple comorbidities, and the quality of the medical care around the operation determines a large share of the outcome. The internist's role spans preoperative risk assessment and risk reduction, timing of surgery, fluid optimisation, anaesthesia-mode selection and secondary-fracture prevention. The evidence for each component is thinner than patients assume, which makes disciplined perioperative optimisation, not any single technique, the real intervention.

teaching_points.claim: Hip fracture is a frequent cause of hospitalisation in the elderly with significant morbidity and mortality, and the internist/hospitalist plays a critical role across preoperative risk assessment, risk reduction, and timing of surgery.

An organised, systematic, coordinated multidisciplinary approach to perioperative management of geriatric surgical patients reduces complications, improves outcomes and lowers cost, and includes work-up and treatment of osteoporosis and fragility fractures.

In proximal femoral fracture, the role of advanced methods of perioperative fluid optimisation (invasive haemodynamic monitoring, protocolised strategies) in reducing risk remains unclear, per a Cochrane review.
Evidence comparing modes of anaesthesia for hip fracture surgery has been limited by heterogeneity in how perioperative outcomes are reported and defined.

uncertainties: Optimal timing of surgery (early versus delayed for medical optimisation) and which preoperative corrections change outcomes.
Whether regional or general anaesthesia meaningfully affects mortality and major complications remains unresolved because of outcome heterogeneity.
mcq_angles: Components of orthogeriatric perioperative optimisation and secondary-fracture prevention.
Timing of surgery: trade-offs between delay for work-up and early fixation.
Evidence limits around anaesthesia mode selection.
Fluid management strategies and the unclear role of invasive haemodynamic monitoring.

A frail patient with CKD and anaemia is listed for hip repair; build the preoperative optimisation checklist and decide what must be corrected before theatre.
page.gaps: Anticoagulation reversal protocols, tranexamic acid use, delirium-prevention bundles and specific nerve-block techniques are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against NICE/AAHKS guidance before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Starting antiretroviral therapy is no longer a decision about whether but about with what and how fast. Contemporary guidelines recommend rapid initiation for everyone diagnosed, and the modern first-line landscape is dominated by integrase-inhibitor single-tablet regimens — above all bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide — chosen for efficacy, high resistance barrier, safety and simplicity. Regimen selection for a treatment-naive adult now turns on comorbidity fit, drug interactions, and how quickly the patient can start, with two-drug simplification reserved for specific maintenance situations.

teaching_points.claim: The 2024 IAS-USA panel updated consensus recommendations for HIV treatment and prevention from 249 relevant citations identified from literature searches.

A systematic literature review and network meta-analysis compares safety outcomes of bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide with other ART regimens in treatment-naive people with HIV-1, addressing a key driver of regimen selection.

Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide is a once-daily single-tablet regimen whose phase 3 trials showed noninferiority to dolutegravir-based therapy; bictegravir is an integrase strand transfer inhibitor with a high genetic barrier to resistance.

Strong evidence supports selected two-drug regimens as a strategy to address long-term toxicity, cost and convenience concerns of lifelong therapy, though not all two-drug combinations are equivalent.

uncertainties: Long-term metabolic effects of integrase inhibitors, including weight gain, are still being characterised.
Eligibility boundaries and durability of two-drug maintenance regimens versus standard three-drug therapy are not fully settled.
mcq_angles: First-line regimen selection in a treatment-naive adult (INSTI-based single-tablet regimens).

page.gaps: Specific dosing tables, HLA-B*5701/abacavir screening, renal and bone monitoring schedules, and TB co-treatment interactions are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against the full IAS-USA 2024 guideline before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Rheumatic complaints in a person with HIV sit at a genuinely three-way diagnostic fork: they may be direct viral or immune-dysregulation effects, musculoskeletal opportunistic infection, or immune reconstitution after starting ART. The spectrum runs from trivial self-limiting arthralgia through seronegative spondyloarthropathy and HIV-associated arthritis to vasculitis and myopathy. ART transformed the whole picture — prevalence patterns shifted and immune-mediated disease re-emerged with immune restoration — so the era in which a patient was treated matters as much as the joint that hurts.

teaching_points.claim: Rheumatic manifestations of HIV encompass arthralgia, HIV-associated arthritis, spondyloarthropathies, inflammatory myopathies, vasculitides and opportunistic musculoskeletal infections, arising from direct viral effects, immune dysregulation, opportunistic infection or ART-induced complications.
With highly active antiretroviral therapy and restored immunity, multiple immune-mediated rheumatic diseases have resurfaced in the HIV population.

Described articular syndromes include HIV-associated arthropathy, seronegative spondyloarthropathies (reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, undifferentiated SpA), rheumatoid arthritis and painful articular syndrome.

Combination ART has normalised life expectancy for adherent patients, so HIV management must now also address long-term complications of HIV and its treatment, including the evolving spectrum of rheumatic syndromes.

uncertainties: Safety and timing of immunosuppression and biologics in patients with untreated or uncontrolled HIV are not well defined.
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome can mimic flares of rheumatic disease, complicating attribution.
mcq_angles: Classifying a joint complaint: direct viral effect, opportunistic infection, or immune reconstitution.

page.mentor_intro: The question 'when should this patient start ART?' has a definitive answer now: immediately, regardless of CD4 count. The trials behind treat-all showed clinical and transmission benefits that ended the CD4-threshold era, and implementation studies such as Eswatini's MaxART trial proved a treat-all strategy is deliverable in real health systems. CD4 counts have not disappeared — they still stratify opportunistic-infection risk and flag advanced disease — but they no longer gate therapy. What remains is execution: same-day starts, linkage to care, and durable suppression, with roughly half of people with HIV worldwide still not on suppressive ART.

teaching_points.claim: Starting ART early, followed by continuous lifetime treatment, most effectively achieves durable virologic suppression and immune restoration, improving clinical outcomes and preventing sexual transmission.
Following randomised trials showing clinical and public-health benefits of immediate initiation, the CD4 count's role has shifted away from deciding when to start ART.

The MaxART Early Access to ART for All trial in Eswatini demonstrated that a Treat-All strategy can be implemented within a government-managed public health system to advance the UNAIDS 90-90-90 targets.
Despite effective therapies, approximately one-half of people with HIV are not receiving suppressive ART.

uncertainties: Same-day ART initiation in patients with advanced disease or opportunistic infections needs individualised timing.
Optimal frequency of CD4 monitoring once a patient is virologically suppressed with a stable count is unresolved across guidelines.

page.mentor_intro: The first visit after a new HIV diagnosis sets the trajectory for everything that follows: confirmatory testing, baseline staging, comorbidity and coinfection screening, and a linkage plan that treats ART start as urgent rather than eventual. Evidence syntheses confirm that ART improves outcomes and reduces transmission, and that interventions compressing the time from diagnosis to treatment initiation measurably raise the proportion who start. The work-up must also see the whole patient — health literacy, stigma and social context predict adherence as strongly as any laboratory value.

teaching_points.claim: Management of newly diagnosed HIV must address health literacy and disease-related stigma, which are barriers to the lifelong treatment engagement required for HIV care.
Updated USPSTF evidence confirms ART is associated with improved clinical outcomes and decreased HIV transmission, underpinning screening-to-treatment linkage.
As policy moved to lifelong ART regardless of CD4 count, pre-ART interventions that improve the rate and timing of treatment initiation became increasingly important, per a systematic review.

uncertainties: The optimal sequencing of baseline testing and same-day ART start versus full work-up first is not standardised.
Which baseline investigations beyond CD4, viral load and resistance testing change management is guideline-dependent.

page.mentor_intro: Opportunistic infections are the price HIV extracts for untreated immunosuppression, and most of that price is avoidable: every major OI is tied to a CD4 threshold that should trigger either prophylaxis or heightened surveillance. Pneumocystis pneumonia remains the canonical example — CD4 below 200 cells/mm3 demands co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, and the same drug treats established disease — while toxoplasmosis, MAC and CMV retinitis each occupy their own strata deeper in the CD4 nadir. With effective ART, the modern skill is not just starting prophylaxis but knowing when stopping is safe.

teaching_points.claim: In HIV-positive patients the risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is strongly correlated with decreased CD4 cell count, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole chemoprophylaxis is highly effective.
Evidence supports discontinuing primary and secondary PJP prophylaxis once CD4 counts have recovered on ART, per a systematic review of discontinuation studies.

TMP-SMX is the first-line agent for treating PJP; dihydropteroate synthase mutations raise potential sulfamide resistance, and PJP still occurs with late presentation or virologic/immunologic failure despite cART.
EACS guideline version 13.0 (2025) was comprehensively revised and reorganised into HIV management/prevention and comorbidity parts, covering first-line regimens and related-infection management.
Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis reduces morbidity and mortality in people with HIV; systematic-review evidence informs WHO guidance on initiation, discontinuation and dose.

uncertainties: Exact CD4 thresholds and required duration of CD4 recovery differ between guidelines for stopping primary versus secondary PJP prophylaxis.
The clinical impact of TMP-SMX resistance mutations on treatment outcomes is incompletely defined.
mcq_angles: PJP prophylaxis threshold (CD4 <200 cells/mm3) and first-line agent (TMP-SMX).
When prophylaxis can be safely discontinued after ART-mediated CD4 recovery.

page.mentor_intro: Pre-exposure prophylaxis is the most powerful prevention tool HIV medicine has ever had, and its failure so far is one of uptake, not efficacy: a daily tenofovir/emtricitabine pill (or two-monthly long-acting cabotegravir, which outperformed the oral standard in a landmark trial) reduces acquisition dramatically in randomised evidence, yet fewer than a fifth of those who could benefit in the US use it. The 2025 Canadian guideline update formalises indications and regimens, and dedicated guidance now addresses populations whose data lagged — notably transgender and nonbinary people, for whom hormone interactions and representation in trials remain live concerns.

teaching_points.claim: The 2025 Canadian guideline updates clinical indications and drug regimens for both PrEP and PEP, drawing on systematic reviews and community-based organisation input.
PrEP effectiveness is well demonstrated in cisgender populations, while empirical data specific to transgender and nonbinary persons remain limited, warranting dedicated clinical guidance.
Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials confirms the clinical effectiveness and safety of oral tenofovir-containing PrEP against HIV acquisition.
Long-acting cabotegravir dosed every 8 weeks has low adherence demands and demonstrated efficacy versus oral TDF/FTC for PrEP; it is the only long-acting agent FDA-approved for HIV PrEP.
A single daily TDF/emtricitabine pill prevents HIV transmission, yet is used by fewer than 20% of people who could benefit in the United States.

uncertainties: Barriers to PrEP uptake and how best to implement long-acting injectable PrEP at scale are unresolved.
Renal and bone monitoring frequency, and drug interactions with gender-affirming hormones, need individualised application.
mcq_angles: PrEP regimen options: daily oral TDF/FTC, long-acting cabotegravir, and their comparative evidence.
Eligibility assessment and key populations, including transgender and nonbinary patients.
Trial evidence for cabotegravir versus oral PrEP.
Monitoring on PrEP: HIV testing, renal function, STI screening.
case_hooks: An MSM patient requests PrEP; choose a regimen and outline baseline assessment and follow-up monitoring.
A patient struggling with daily oral adherence asks about alternatives; discuss long-acting cabotegravir and its initiation schedule.
page.gaps: On-demand (2-1-1) dosing, STI screening intervals, renal monitoring protocols and pregnancy-related guidance are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against the full Canadian 2025 guideline before approval.
